Whole-lesson orientation

Overview

Lecture pp. 2-3, 93-100

What this laboratory expects you to recognize

  • Type, name, and classification of a tumor from morphologic features.
  • Morphologic characteristics of cancer cells on gross and microscopic material.
  • Benign versus malignant behavior from cytologic and morphologic clues.
  • Grading and staging as they relate to prognosis, biological behavior, and survival.
  • Recognition of gross and microscopic morphology of formalin-fixed surgical specimens.
Must Know Framework

Nomenclature → Gross → Microscopic → Histogenesis → Grade → Behavior → Prognosis → Treatment.

More undifferentiated generally means a more aggressive tumor in the lecture review pointers.

Lab Ex. A1

Leiomyoma, Uterus

Lecture pp. 4-12

Case anchor

A 43-year-old female had heavy menstrual bleeding and dysmenorrhea. Imaging showed a submucous leiomyoma, followed by hysterectomy.

Core identity

  • Benign neoplasm of uterine smooth muscle.
  • May be multiple in the myometrium.
  • Lecture specimens include TAHBSO material with uterus, ovaries, and fallopian tubes.
Key Differentiator

Gross: white to tan-white, whorled, firm, bulging cut surface.

Microscopy: intersecting or interlacing fascicles of monotonous spindle cells with cigar-shaped nuclei.

Gross morphology

  • Well-defined and round.
  • Well-circumscribed but nonencapsulated in a lecture specimen.
  • Firm with a bulging cut surface.
  • Classic whorled pattern.
  • A sample submucous lesion measured 5 cm and protruded into the uterine cavity.

Microscopic morphology

  • Intersecting or interlacing fascicles of monotonous spindle cells.
  • Cell borders are indistinct.
  • Cytoplasm is eosinophilic.
  • Nuclei are cigar shaped with small nucleoli.
  • Atypia is absent or mild.
  • Mitoses are rare.
High-Yield Recap

Leiomyoma = benign smooth muscle tumor with well-circumscribed whorled gross morphology and bland spindle cells with cigar-shaped nuclei.

The lecture contrast emphasizes slow growth, localized behavior, and lack of metastasis.

Lab Ex. A2

Osteogenic Sarcoma, Bone

Lecture pp. 13-28

Case anchor

An 18-year-old male had progressive painful enlargement of the lower thigh. The mass measured about 12 × 10 cm. X-ray showed a mixed lytic and osteoblastic mass at the distal femur.

Core identity

  • Malignant, high-grade bone tumor.
  • Diagnostic concept: tumor cells produce osteoid.
  • Lecture material describes a malignant mesenchymal tumor of bone.
Must Know

There has to be demonstration of osteoid produced by neoplastic or malignant osteoblasts to make the diagnosis of osteosarcoma in the lecture.

Gross morphology

  • Typically large and bulky.
  • Tan-white, firm, and gritty on cut surface.
  • May contain areas of hemorrhage and cystic degeneration.
  • Margins are permeative and ill defined.
  • Can break through the cortex, elevate the periosteum, and infiltrate surrounding soft tissue.
  • Can extend into the epiphysis.

Location and spread pattern

  • Originates in the medullary cavity close to the metaphyseal plate.
  • Spreads extensively within the medullary cavity.
  • Eventually erodes through the cortical plate and extends into soft tissue.
  • Grows rapidly and metastasizes early via the bloodstream.
  • The lecture highlights the lungs as the usual metastatic site.

Lecture-supported invasion sequence

Metaphysis
Intramedullary origin
→
Medullary cavity
Rapid expansion
→
Cortex
Destruction and permeation
→
Periosteum
Elevation and reaction
→
Soft tissue
Infiltration
→
Bloodstream
Early lung metastasis
Radiographic Cue

An ill-defined cloud-like lesion may be seen in the distal femur.

Codman triangle is described as a triangular shell of reactive bone between cortex and periosteum due to periosteal elevation.

Microscopic morphology

  • Malignant osteoid may be thin and lace-like or broad and irregular.
  • Osteoid is deposited between anaplastic cells.
  • Tumor cells are pleomorphic, often larger than normal osteoblasts, with hyperchromatic nuclei.
  • Increased nuclear and nucleolar size with increased N/C ratio.
  • High mitotic activity with abnormal mitoses.
  • Osteoclast-like giant cells may be present.
High-Yield Recap

Osteosarcoma = malignant mesenchymal bone tumor with direct osteoid production by malignant cells.

Think metaphysis, destructive infiltrative growth, gritty tan-white mass, cortex and soft-tissue invasion, and early hematogenous lung metastasis.

Lab Ex. A Guide Questions

Mesenchymal Tumor Principles

Lecture pp. 29-32
FeatureBenign example: LeiomyomaMalignant example: Osteosarcoma
DifferentiationWell differentiated.Poorly differentiated and anaplastic.
GrossSmall and well demarcated.
Whorling pattern.
Non-invasive.		Irregular and infiltrative borders.
Necrosis may be present.
CellsNormal N/C ratio.
Cells resemble normal tissue.		Abnormal N/C ratio.
Pleomorphism.
Hyperchromatism and loss of polarity.

Biological behavior: benign versus malignant counterpart

  • Benign leiomyoma: resembles tissue of origin and is well differentiated.
  • Slow growing, circumscribed, and described as encapsulated in the guide table.
  • Likely to retain normal functions and remain localized.
  • Malignant leiomyosarcoma: poorly differentiated or anaplastic.
  • Rapid growth, poor circumscription, invasion of healthy tissue, and distant metastasis.

Route of metastasis

  • Mesenchymal malignancies: hematogenous spread is more typical of sarcomas.
  • Penetration usually involves small veins because arteries have thicker walls.
  • Carcinomas: usual route is lymphatic spread.
  • The sentinel lymph node is the first node receiving lymph flow from the primary tumor.
  • The lecture highlights liver and lungs as common sites in hematogenous dissemination.
Tumor Nomenclature

Benign tumors: commonly use the suffix -oma.

Malignant epithelial tumors: use -carcinoma.

Malignant mesenchymal tumors: use -sarcoma.

Lecture exceptions to the reassuring sound of “-oma” include melanoma, lymphoma, mesothelioma, and hepatoma.

Lab Ex. B1

Tubular Adenoma, Colon

Lecture pp. 33-43

Case anchor

A 36-year-old asymptomatic female with a strong family history of colon carcinoma had a 1.0 cm polyp in the transverse colon on endoscopy.

Core identity

  • Benign gland-forming tumor.
  • A neoplastic polyp with at least low-grade dysplasia.
  • Diagnosis requires histologic confirmation of dysplasia.
Must Know

Dysplasia is the cellular change that distinguishes a benign neoplastic adenomatous polyp from a non-neoplastic polyp in the lecture guide questions.

Gross morphology

  • May be pedunculated or sessile.
  • Smooth outer surface.
  • Appears dark red compared with surrounding mucosa.
  • Lecture specimens also show multiple small sessile polyps on colonic mucosa.

Dysplastic epithelial features

  • Hyperchromatic nuclei extending toward the surface.
  • Nuclear crowding and pseudostratification.
  • Nuclei may be enlarged, elongated, and elliptical or cigar shaped.
  • Cells remain relatively uniform and maintain polarity in low-grade dysplasia.
  • Goblet cells are reduced.
  • Nucleoli are not prominent.

Normal versus adenomatous epithelium

Normal colonic epitheliumSmall round nuclei.
Abundant goblet cells.
Adenoma architecturePolypoid growth composed of regular glands lined by columnar epithelium.
Low-grade dysplasiaHypercellularity, crowded elongated hyperchromatic nuclei, decreased goblet cell mucin, and retained polarity.
Key Differentiator

The lecture identifies tubular adenoma as a premalignant lesion and a precursor to invasive adenocarcinoma.

Lab Ex. B2

Adenocarcinoma, Colon

Lecture pp. 44-53

Case anchor

A 56-year-old male with blood-streaked stool and changes in stool pattern had a large colonic mass. Biopsy showed adenocarcinoma and colon resection followed.

Key Differentiator

Infiltration or invasion and metastasis are histologic and biological evidence of malignant transformation in the lecture.

Gross morphology

  • Bulky, fungating or polypoid mass.
  • May be friable.
  • Can obstruct or obliterate the lumen.
  • Invades the colonic wall and may extend into pericolic fat.
  • Lecture specimens may show multiple small polyps elsewhere in the mucosa.

Histologic morphology

  • Irregular complex glands with severe dysplasia.
  • Irregular tumor glands infiltrate muscularis propria and pericolic fat.
  • Desmoplastic reaction means increased fibrosis around advancing tumor cells.
  • The lecture demonstrates adenocarcinoma arising in an adenomatous polyp.

Lecture pattern: adenoma to invasive carcinoma

Tubular adenoma
Neoplastic polyp
→
Dysplasia
At least low grade
→
Adenocarcinoma
Irregular malignant glands
→
Invasion
Muscularis propria and pericolic fat
→
Metastasis
Lymph node involvement shown in lecture
Must Know

A lecture lymph-node specimen shows metastatic adenocarcinoma, including highly dysplastic tumor cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and limited gland formation.

Lab Ex. B3

Squamous Cell Carcinoma

Lecture pp. 54-71

Case anchor: penis

A 60-year-old male had a penile mass for 4 years with recent enlargement. Biopsy showed a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.

The lecture also demonstrates gross squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix and histologic squamous cell carcinoma using skin and cervical material.

Must Know

Keratin pearls and intercellular bridges are central evidence of squamous differentiation in the lecture.

Abundant keratin pearls support a well-differentiated Grade 1 tumor.

Gross morphology

  • Malignant tumor of squamous cell origin.
  • May appear as a large nodule, a round lesion with central hyperkeratosis, an ulcerated lesion, or a verrucous or cauliflower-like mass.
  • Penile specimen: fungating mass involving glans and shaft.
  • Borders are infiltrative with adjacent structure encroachment.
  • Cervical specimen: irregular, ulcerating, partly papillary growth involving ectocervix and endocervix.

Microscopic morphology

  • Atypical squamous cells arising from dysplastic epithelium.
  • Pleomorphism and hyperchromatic nuclei.
  • Eosinophilic cytoplasm with prominent nucleoli.
  • Increased mitoses and abnormal mitoses.
  • Marked keratinization with keratin pearl formation.
  • Intercellular bridges.
  • Invasion into adjacent tissue.

Histogenesis clues

  • Cell type: epithelial and produces keratin.
  • Architecture: sheets or islands of tumor cells.
  • Cytoplasm: eosinophilic and pleomorphic with prominent nucleoli.
  • Stroma: sparse fibrotic stroma with inflammatory infiltrate.

Normal skin orientation

  • Keratin overlies the epidermis.
  • Epidermal layers are organized and prominent.
  • Hair follicles, arrector pili muscle, and sebaceous glands are present in the dermis.
  • Lecture epidermal layers: stratum corneum, lucidum, granulosum, spinosum, and basale.
High-Yield Recap

Squamous cell carcinoma = malignant squamous tumor with keratinization, keratin pearls, intercellular bridges, pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, increased N/C ratio, high mitotic rate, abnormal mitoses, and invasion.

Lab Ex. B Guide Questions

Epithelial Tumor Principles

Lecture pp. 72-78
Adenoma versus Non-neoplastic Polyp

Dysplasia is the distinguishing cellular change in the lecture.

Non-neoplastic polyps such as inflammatory polyps do not have this cancerous potential in the lecture explanation.

Evidence of Malignant Transformation

Metastasis: spread to a distant, noncontiguous site.

Infiltration or invasion: tumor expands into surrounding tissues.

FeatureAdenocarcinomaSquamous Cell Carcinoma
Cell originLining of ducts and glands.Squamous epithelium.
Precursor or premalignant lesionAdenoma or dysplasia.Carcinoma in situ, dysplasia, dyskeratosis, or actinic keratosis.
Actual grade shownWell differentiated, Grade 1.Well differentiated, Grade 1.

Grading

  • Degree of differentiation of the tumor.
  • Measures the extent to which tumor cells resemble or fail to resemble their normal counterparts.
  • Higher grade corresponds to a more aggressive tumor in the lecture.

Staging

  • Based on primary tumor size or lesion extent T.
  • Regional lymph-node spread N.
  • Presence or absence of distant metastasis M.
  • Higher grade and stage are associated with poorer prognosis in the lecture.

Lab Ex. C1

Wilms Tumor (Nephroblastoma), Kidney

Lecture pp. 79-85

Case anchor

A 6-year-old girl had an abdominal mass. Imaging showed a left-sided renal mass.

Core identity

  • Malignant embryonal tumor originating from nephrogenic blastema.
  • Imitates the histology of the developing kidney.
  • Thought in the lecture to develop from persistent metanephric tissue or nephrogenic rests.
Must Know

The characteristic pattern is triphasic: blastemal, epithelial, and stromal components.

An increased proportion of the blastemal component renders the tumor more malignant in the lecture.

Gross morphology

  • Large and well demarcated.
  • Bulging, fleshy, and lobulated.
  • Lecture description: yellow-tan.

Triphasic microscopic pattern

  • Blastemal: solid sheets of small round cells.
  • Epithelial: abortive tubules and related primitive structures.
  • Stromal: mesenchymal or fibroblast-like tissue.
ComponentDifferentiation and morphology
BlastemaLeast differentiated.
Small to medium undifferentiated cells.
Higher proportion is associated with greater malignancy in the lecture.
EpithelialRosette-like structures: poorly differentiated.
Tubules and papillary structures: moderately differentiated.
Glomerular-like structures and small mature tubules: well differentiated.
StromalMost differentiated.
Cells have indistinct borders with oval to spindle-shaped nuclei and bland nucleoli.
High-Yield Recap

Wilms tumor = nephroblastoma arising from metanephric blastemal cells, with the classic blastema + epithelial + stroma triphasic pattern.

Lab Ex. C2

Dermoid Cyst, Ovary

Lecture pp. 86-90

Case anchor

A 25-year-old G0P0 female had vague right-sided abdominal pain and a palpable right lower-quadrant mass. Ultrasound showed a 15 cm ovarian cystic complex mass.

Core identity

  • Teratoma of a cystic nature.
  • Originates from pluripotent or totipotential germ cells.
  • Also called a mature or benign cystic teratoma in the lecture guide material.
Key Differentiator

Recognition depends on mature differentiated tissues, especially skin-type elements such as squamous epithelium, hair follicles, and sebaceous glands.

Gross morphology

  • Thin cyst wall.
  • Usually smooth but may have a knob-like nodular protrusion.
  • The nodule may contain cartilage, bone, teeth, or adipose tissue.
  • Lecture specimens show clumps of hair, teeth, and thick sebaceous material.

Histologic morphology

  • Differentiation along ectodermal lines can create a cyst lined by skin.
  • Benign squamous epithelium.
  • Sebaceous glands and hair follicles.
  • Tooth structures may be present.
  • Ovarian stroma is shown at the periphery in a lecture slide.
High-Yield Recap

Dermoid cyst = benign mature cystic teratoma from totipotent germ cells, commonly displaying mature tissues such as skin, hair, sebaceous glands, teeth, cartilage, and fat.

Final rapid review

Cram Sheet

Final tab
Fastest Malignancy Screen

Gross: ill-defined, infiltrative, irregular, necrotic, hemorrhagic, or ulcerated.

Microscopic: pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, high N/C ratio, prominent nucleoli, increased or atypical mitoses, loss of polarity, abnormal architecture, and invasion.

Biologic proof: invasion and metastasis.

Leiomyoma

  • Benign smooth muscle tumor of uterus.
  • Whorled, firm, white-tan, well-circumscribed mass.
  • Interlacing spindle-cell fascicles.
  • Cigar-shaped nuclei.
  • Atypia absent or mild.
    Mitoses rare.

Osteogenic Sarcoma

  • Malignant high-grade bone tumor.
  • Think metaphysis, gritty tan-white destructive mass.
  • Diagnostic: malignant cells produce osteoid.
  • Breaks cortex, elevates periosteum, invades soft tissue.
  • Hematogenous spread with early lung metastasis.

Tubular Adenoma

  • Benign gland-forming neoplastic polyp.
  • At least low-grade dysplasia.
  • Crowded elongated hyperchromatic nuclei.
  • Reduced goblet cells.
  • Premalignant precursor to invasive adenocarcinoma.

Colon Adenocarcinoma

  • Bulky, fungating or polypoid mass.
  • May obstruct lumen and invade pericolic fat.
  • Irregular complex glands with severe dysplasia.
  • Desmoplasia at advancing tumor.
  • Lecture demonstrates lymph-node metastasis.

Squamous Cell Carcinoma

  • Malignant tumor of squamous epithelium.
  • Keratin pearls and intercellular bridges.
  • Pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, prominent nucleoli.
  • Increased and abnormal mitoses.
  • Abundant keratin pearls → well differentiated Grade 1.

Wilms Tumor

  • Nephroblastoma from metanephric blastema.
  • Malignant embryonal tumor of kidney.
  • Triphasic: blastema + epithelial + stroma.
  • Blastema is least differentiated.
  • More blastema → more malignant in the lecture.

Dermoid Cyst

  • Mature or benign cystic teratoma.
  • From totipotential germ cells.
  • Thin cyst wall with possible nodular protrusion.
  • Hair, sebaceous material, teeth, cartilage, bone, or fat may be seen.
  • Histology often shows benign squamous lining with skin appendages.

Grade versus Stage

  • Grade = differentiation and resemblance to normal counterpart.
  • Stage = TNM extent of disease.
  • T primary tumor.
    N regional nodes.
    M distant metastasis.
  • Higher grade and stage → poorer prognosis in lecture guidance.

Irregular malignant glands invading muscularis or pericolic fat + desmoplasiaColon adenocarcinoma.
Keratin pearls + intercellular bridgesSquamous cell carcinoma.
Blastema + abortive tubules + stromaWilms tumor.
Ovarian cyst with skin, hair, sebaceous glands, teeth, or other mature tissuesDermoid cyst / mature cystic teratoma.

Exam Traps from the Lecture

Not every “-oma” is benign. Melanoma, lymphoma, seminoma, hepatoma, and other lecture exceptions break the naming shortcut.

Keratin pearls tell grade, not stage. Abundant keratin pearls support a well-differentiated Grade 1 squamous cell carcinoma, but do not by themselves establish Stage 1.

Osteoclasts do not establish osteosarcoma. The key diagnostic support is osteoid formation by tumor cells.
